title: A Man Apart
full_review:
"A Man Apart" (New Line) is a testosterone-driven crime drama about a Los Angeles Drug Enforcement Agency agent (Vin Diesel) bent on avenging his wife's murder by taking down the powerful Mexican drug cartel responsible for her death.

The action flick is directed by F. Gary Gray, who cut his teeth in the content-thin world of music videos. Unfortunately, the narrative follows the all-too-common recipe of two parts gratuitous violence, two parts stylish visuals, with dollops of biceps and bare breasts and not more than a pinch of plot thrown in for good measure -- then mix and let sit as the body-count rises.

Sean Vetter (Diesel) is a cop with a volatile, brass-knuckle attitude, the lead dog of a narcotics unit dubbed "the gunslingers" for their unconventional albeit highly effective tactics. Having traded in the gang colors of his youth for a shiny gold badge, he still lives by the code that helped him survive on the mean streets of Los Angeles. Along with his childhood friend and now partner, Demetrius Hicks (Larenz Tate), Vetter has waged a seven-year war to stem the virulent tide of drugs flowing into the country from Mexico. Their perseverance pays off when they nab the notorious Baja Cartel kingpin, Memo Lucero (Geno Silva), in a raid south of the border.

With Lucero safely locked away, the brooding Vetter can hang up his bulletproof vest, return home and reveal his kinder-gentler side, frolicking in a picturesque Malibu sunset with his candle-making wife, Stacy (Jacqueline Obradors).

But Vetter's serenity is short-lived. Having only cut off the head of the multibillion dollar hydra, a new, more ruthless, figure known only as Diablo emerges to violently claim the lucrative cartel .Unwilling to see their years of hard work go for naught, Vetter and his team set their sights on the enigmatic new player. Diablo, however, has Vetter in his own cross-hairs. Tragedy strikes when, during an assassination attempt on Vetter, Diablo's henchmen kill Stacy.

Robbed of the only thing that gave his life meaning, Vetter embarks on a personal vendetta against Diablo, employing any means necessary to exact his revenge, including an unlikely alliance with the jailed cartel boss, Lucero. Vetter relentlessly pursues Diablo edging dangerously close to the tenuous boundary separating justice from vengeance, even at the expense of the laws he has sworn to uphold and protect.

The film's incessant violence is disturbing, especially in the current climate where world events expose the ugly reality of violence and its consequences as opposed to the stylized version offered by Hollywood. In orchestrating scene after scene of video game-like shoot-'em-ups, the filmmakers display an almost cavalier disregard for human life, using actors like props to be mowed down like ducks at a carnival game. In one particular sequence it is difficult to distinguish the good guys from the bad guys -- a trifle sure to be overlooked by audiences hungry for a steady diet of ammo and pyrotechnics and growing increasingly anesthetized by the ever-escalating sophistication of choreographed carnage on film.

Also disconcerting is the positive portrayal of the character Big Sexy (George Sharperson), a mountainous drug dealer with a teddy-bear smile. He is a member of Vetter's posse since childhood; they have remained close, despite being on opposite sides of the law. It seemed quite inconsistent that after combating the drug trafficking so doggedly, Vetter never so much as questions Big Sexy's involvement in the death trade that not only ruins countless lives, but took the life of Stacy.

The moral dilemma presented -- justice vs. revenge -- does add a hint of drama to an otherwise hackneyed narrative. Fans of the crime genre would be better advised to view last year's "Narc," which explored the theme more effectively.

At one point in the film the incarcerated Lucero advises that to destroy a monster like Diablo Vetter must dispense with the rules and "become a monster." While supplying the filmmakers with the catchy tagline, this ends-justifies-the-means mentality is incompatible with the Christian understanding of overcoming evil with good.

All in all, this Diesel, unfortunately, is running on empty.

Due to excessive graphic violence, sleazy sexual situations with partial nudity and incessant rough language and profanities, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
